chapter_theme: Forbearance as strength: it wins the victory, it outlasts revenge's one day of pleasure, and for those who can bear harsh words it outranks fasting. Beyond it lies forgetting the wrong entirely.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: forbearance's excellence (151-154), bearing what others do (155-158), and bearing what others say (159-160).

151.reading: Like the earth that holds up those who dig into it, bearing with those who scorn you is the highest thing.
151.nuance: Parimelazhagar's gloss brings out the image: the earth keeps the digger from falling, so the one injured is still supporting the one who injures. Forbearance here is more than not responding.

152.reading: Always bear with excess against you; forgetting it is better still.
152.nuance: Parimelazhagar explains why forgetting ranks higher: to forbear, one must still hold the wrong in mind. He adds that one should forbear even when one has the power to punish, which is what makes this more than helplessness.

153.reading: The poverty of poverties is turning away a guest, and the strength of strengths is forbearance toward fools.
153.nuance: The verse is an analogy, as Parimelazhagar notes: just as turning a guest away isn't wealth, bearing with fools isn't weakness. The first half is there to change what we think the second half means.

positions.position: விருந்து means a guest, and turning one away is the worst poverty.
positions.quote: வறுமையுள் வைத்து வறுமையாவது விருந்தினரை ஏற்றுக் கொள்ளாது நீக்குதல்;

positions.position: விருந்து means novelty: the weakest weakness is failing to reject the strange and unheard-of.

154.reading: If you want நிறை never to leave you, keep and live by forbearance.
154.nuance: Forbearance is presented as the means, and நிறை is what is at stake. Parimelazhagar takes the latter as worth of character, and Manakkudavar as a guarded discipline: keeping what should be kept and rejecting what should be rejected.

155.reading: They don't count at all those who retaliate, but those who forbear they keep wrapped up like gold.
155.nuance: It's a claim about social estimation, which is why the motive is reputational. Parimelazhagar gives the reason: the person who retaliates has become the wrongdoer's equal. He reads 'wrapping up' as constantly bearing them in mind.

156.reading: Those who retaliate have one day's joy, and those who forbear have renown until they perish.
156.nuance: The verse honestly concedes that revenge is a pleasure. Parimelazhagar plays this down with 'false joy'.

positions.position: The word 'world' is supplied, so the renown lasts until the world itself ends.
The renown lasts as long as the forbearing person lives.

157.reading: Though others do you wrong, it's good to feel the pain of it and not do what is contrary to virtue.
157.nuance: நோநொந்து, grieving at the pain, doesn't say whose pain. On the first reading below, the wronged person pities the wrongdoer, which is a remarkable demand.

positions.position: One grieves for the suffering that will come to the wrongdoer, who may fall into hell.
One feels hurt by the base act done to oneself, and still does not take revenge.

158.reading: Those who do wrong out of their excess, defeat them by your own rightness.
158.nuance: The language is of winning. Manakkudavar says it most directly: forbearing isn't defeat, it is victory. மிகுதி and தகுதி, excess and fitness, are set against each other as rival kinds of power.

159.reading: Those who bear the harsh words from the mouths of those who go beyond bounds are as pure as those who have renounced.
159.nuance: Parimelazhagar spells out the implication: this is someone still in household life. The purity of renunciation can therefore be reached without renouncing. Here இறந்தார் means those who overstep, not the dead.

160.reading: Those who fast are great, but only after those who bear what others say in harshness.
160.nuance: The verse first grants greatness and then takes the top rank away. Parimelazhagar's reasoning is subtle: bearing insult is done while one's sense of 'I' and 'mine' is still in place, the very things that make it hard.

links.note: Both set a kind of endurance above the ascetic's. 48 says the householder endures more because he also bears others' pain, and 160 says that bearing harsh words comes first. Each reassigns the word நோன்பு or நோன்மை to a life in society.

நிறை appears in 57 as a woman's inner guard, and here it's what anyone stands to lose without forbearance. The same inner discipline is asked of women as chastity and of people in general as character.
Both call refusal of a guest a kind of poverty. 89 says so directly, and 153 uses it as an analogy for something else, which shows that this was a settled saying that could be drawn on.

Both say that forgetting is what's best. On Parimelazhagar's reading of 108 it's narrowly about one who has also done good. Verse 152 removes that limit, and gives forgetting a rank above forbearance.
157 asks for not retaliating, and 314 goes further: punish the wrongdoer by doing him good so that he's ashamed. What starts as restraint becomes a strategy.

Two verses, for different reasons, place the ascetic's hunger second. In 160 it's after bearing insults, and in 225 it's after relieving others' hunger. The book keeps finding what's greater than fasting.

source_issues: The Tamil of verse 153 in kg/core reads இன்நம்யுள், a typo for இன்மையுள். The Tamil of verse 154 reads பொநற்யுடைமை, a typo for பொறையுடைமை.
Manakkudavar's gloss on verse 153 ('புதுமையை நீக் காமை') may reflect a different understanding of விருந்தொரால், and is worth checking.
Manakkudavar is not aligned for verses 152 and 159.
